title: The Statue of Liberty
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World). They cover Édouard de Laboulaye's idea as a centennial gift from France, sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi's reuse of an earlier Egyptian lighthouse design, the choice of Bedloe Island, the Franco-American Union and its fundraising, engineer Gustave Eiffel's wrought-iron internal skeleton, the pantograph and pointing-up enlargement method, the copper skin and pedestal, Joseph Pulitzer's newspaper crowdfunding drive, Emma Lazarus's poem "The New Colossus," the 1886 dedication, the green patina, the 1980s restoration, and visitor access today. Also includes a short listener mail segment and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with a joking exchange about the statue and introduce the full name Liberty Enlightening the World.

segments.title: Origins of the idea and the French gift
segments.summary: The idea is traced to Édouard de Laboulaye, who wanted to honor America's progress around 1865 and give a gift for the 1876 centennial. The statue was paid for by donations rather than given by the French government.

segments.title: Bartholdi's design and Egyptian origins
segments.summary: Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi reused an earlier design made for an Egyptian lighthouse in the Suez Canal. He changed the headdress to a spiked crown, swapped the lamp for a torch, and added the tablet inscribed with July 4, 1776. Details at the feet include broken shackles and chains.

segments.title: Choosing Bedloe Island and the Franco-American Union
segments.summary: Bartholdi visited America in 1871 and chose Bedloe Island as the site, later renamed Liberty Island in 1956. He helped found the Franco-American Union to raise private support. A tangent discusses Franco American spaghetti.

segments.title: Visiting the statue and Bartholdi's model
segments.summary: The hosts discuss not having visited the statue, a Radiohead concert near it in 2001, and the legend that Bartholdi used Jeanne-Émilie Baheux as the model for the face or body, with his mother's face possibly used.

segments.title: Engineering: Viollet-le-Duc and Eiffel's iron skeleton
segments.summary: Bartholdi consulted architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, who suggested a concrete core and a copper skin made with repoussé. After Viollet-le-Duc died, Gustave Eiffel proposed a lighter wrought-iron truss and girder skeleton around a central pylon. The statue can sway about three inches and the torch about six.

segments.title: Scaling up: pantograph and pointing up
segments.summary: The team enlarged a tabletop model with pantographs up to one quarter size, then used plumb lines and string at around 300 main reference points (about 9,000 measurements) to scale up to full size, a technique called pointing up.

segments.title: Building the copper skin and pedestal
segments.summary: Plaster molds and wooden forms shaped the thin copper sheets, which were hammered into place and riveted. Pierre Eugène Secretan donated copper. The pedestal is a concrete truncated pyramid faced with Connecticut granite, anchored with steel beams.

segments.title: Fundraising in France and America and Pulitzer's campaign
segments.summary: France raised funds through lotteries, school contributions, and banquets held inside the statue's sections. Americans fell short, and Joseph Pulitzer's newspaper ran a small-donation campaign that exceeded its goal. Emma Lazarus's poem The New Colossus was written for the fundraising and later engraved on a plaque.

segments.title: Dedication, patina, restoration, and access today
segments.summary: The statue was shipped in crates, reassembled, and dedicated October 28, 1886 (the hosts say October 6), with a flag-drop mishap. The copper turned green through patina, the torch was replaced during a restoration, and the iron was swapped for stainless steel. Visitors can reach the crown by stairs, and the torch has been closed to visitors since 1960.

segments.title: Listener mail: Alyssa Stewart
segments.summary: A fourteen-year-old listener from northern Utah asks for her letter to be read to her siblings.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and point listeners to the Stuff Podcasts email for mail requests.
